prompt: Build the home page for Fernhollow Seed Library, a volunteer-run library where neighbours borrow packets of heirloom vegetable and flower seeds and return seeds saved from their own plots. Opening hours Tue/Thu 4-7pm and Sat 10-1 at the old grange hall. Include a headline, a short intro, how borrowing works in three steps, the hours, and a plain join-the-mailing-list line. It should feel warm, handmade and trustworthy, not corporate. One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, nothing loaded from outside.
rubric: The typefaces are chosen to fit a warm, handmade, trustworthy library (for example a humane serif or soft text face for the headline), not a default corporate sans used everywhere
Every font-family declaration ends in a sensible generic fallback and names only fonts that can plausibly exist as installed system fonts; no @import, link or url() to external fonts
Headline and body clearly use different roles (size, weight or face) while the page stays within two families at most
Body text is comfortably readable in the screenshot: sensible size, line length and contrast, not a thin or condensed face
The page has no external assets and renders fully offline with all requested content present (headline, intro, three steps, hours, mailing-list line)

prompt: We're a two-person startup building Hollin Ledger, payroll and seasonal-worker timesheets for small farms. Mostly used on cheap Android phones and old office laptops, often on bad rural connections. We have basically no budget for font licences and our designer said to keep the whole page weight small. What typefaces should we use for the app and for the marketing site? Give me something I can paste in.
rubric: Recommends concrete typefaces or stacks for both the app and the marketing site, with CSS that can be pasted, rather than only describing qualities
Respects the licence constraint: every named family is system-installed or openly licensed, and licence status is stated or clearly implied honestly
Respects the weight constraint: limits the number of families, weights or files and says whether to self-host, subset or rely on system fonts
Includes a fallback stack that falls to a real generic family and explains what happens on the cheap Android and old-laptop case
Is honest about uncertainty (e.g. which system fonts are actually present on which devices) instead of asserting that a font is installed everywhere
Gives a short reasoned choice rather than a long menu of undifferentiated options

prompt: Our night shift at Brannock Cold Storage checks stock on rugged scanners that run old Windows with a small screen, wearing gloves, in poor light. Make me a stock-check page: a table of about 12 rows with SKU, bin location, expected quantity, counted quantity (an input), and a status. Add a search box on top. Single HTML file, inline CSS, nothing from the internet.
rubric: Uses plain, highly legible system fonts suited to a work tool; no decorative, script or novelty display face and no attempt to load a webfont
SKUs, bin codes and quantities are easy to tell apart character by character (for example a monospaced or clearly distinguishable face, and aligned figures in the quantity columns)
Type is large enough and contrasty enough for gloves and poor light: table text and inputs are not tiny
The font stack lists fallbacks that exist on old Windows and ends in a generic family
The page is a usable dense table with all requested columns, a search box, and about 12 rows, with no external assets

prompt: Our marketing site loads a custom font and for a split second everything is in a different font and then the whole page jumps when ours arrives. Sometimes the headline is just invisible for a second. Why does that happen and what should we actually do about it? We use one variable font file for headings and the system font for body text.
rubric: Explains the cause correctly: the browser shows fallback text or hides text while the file downloads, and the metric differences between the fallback and the loaded font cause the visible shift
Names a concrete fix for invisible text (a font-display setting or equivalent) and says which behavior it produces
Addresses the jump itself with a concrete technique such as adjusting fallback metrics, choosing a closer fallback, preloading, or reducing the swap to headings only
Applies the answer to their actual setup (one heading file, system body text) instead of generic advice about many fonts
Gives short copy-pasteable CSS or markup and does not claim the problem can be eliminated entirely in every browser

prompt: Kettlewick Tea imports single-estate teas and sells to customers in Poland, Vietnam and Turkey as well as the UK. Product names include things like Đại Hồng Bào, Żółta Herbata and Çay Rize with the original spellings kept. The shop is being rebuilt and the designer picked a very stylish display font from a free font site for headings. Is that fine? What should we pick or check?
rubric: Identifies that the supplied display font must be checked for the accented and Vietnamese stacked-diacritic characters actually used, naming concrete characters or the Latin Extended coverage needed
Explains what goes wrong when coverage is missing (fallback glyphs from another face, missing characters or mismatched weight) and how to test it with the real product names
Gives a practical way to decide: either confirm coverage, or choose a face known to cover the needed Latin ranges, or limit the display font to text that is safe, with a fallback for the rest
Mentions line-height or clipping risk for tall stacked diacritics in headings
Does not simply approve or condemn the stylish font without looking at the coverage question, and is honest about what cannot be verified from the name alone
Recognises that the setup is already sound and says so plainly rather than inventing problems
Leaves the existing stacks and roles essentially intact; any change is small, optional and clearly marked as such
Does not rewrite the system to a different font strategy or add webfonts, extra families or external loading
If it suggests anything, the suggestion is accurate and specific (for example one concrete tweak), not a long list of generic improvements
Answer is brief and proportionate to a review that finds almost nothing to fix

prompt: Quick one, answer in two sentences max: for our API docs site (lots of prose and code samples, mostly developers on laptops) is it fine to just use the system font stack and a system monospace, or do we need to pay for a nice font?
rubric: Answer is at most two sentences
Gives a direct yes/no style answer: the system stacks are fine for this audience and no paid font is required
Mentions code samples getting the system monospace or a monospace stack in a way that is accurate
Does not hedge into a list, headings, bullets or an offer of a long follow-up in place of the short answer
Judges the setup honestly as a problem for the actual task (parents reading hours and prices on phones), not just as unfashionable
Flags the too-many-faces issue by counting the display families in use (four) and the load cost of fetching all of them
Flags that the body text is a hairline weight at a small size and that the opening hours are set in a script face at 11px
Notes the missing generic fallbacks and the dependence on an external request for text that must always be readable

Keeps what is worth keeping: acknowledges that playful character suits a children's museum, and proposes a smaller concrete direction (for example one friendly display face for headings only with a plain body face) rather than only saying no
Delivers a clear next-step fix with replacement CSS or font names, in plain language for a non-expert

prompt: Lantern Row Library is putting a self-service kiosk in the lobby: a 15-inch touchscreen, viewed standing up from about half a metre, used by everyone from kids to older readers. Screens: search by title or author, book result cards (title, author, shelf code like 'QB 412.7', due date, copies available), a check-out confirmation, and a receipt. I need a type plan: which kind of face for which job, how many families, and what to do about the shelf codes and due dates. No fonts have to be downloaded; the kiosk runs a locked-down browser with whatever system fonts the OS image has.
rubric: Assigns typeface roles to the named screens and elements (titles, authors, shelf codes, due dates, buttons, receipt), not just a general style paragraph
Keeps to a small number of families and justifies it for a kiosk viewed at distance by a wide age range
Specifies how shelf codes and dates are made unambiguous to read and copy (for example distinguishable characters, aligned or fixed-width figures) and says why
Handles the locked-down system-fonts constraint with a fallback stack and a concrete step to check which fonts the OS image actually has
Notes size and weight needs for standing distance and mixed ages with concrete starting values presented as starting points to test, not as guarantees

prompt: Our designer showed me the new site on her MacBook and it looks crisp and lovely. When I open it on my Windows work PC the text looks thinner and a bit rough, and on my sister's old Android tablet the headings are in a totally different font. Same URL. What's going on, and what should we test before launch? We use a font stack that starts with Helvetica Neue.
rubric: Explains correctly that different operating systems render the same font differently (smoothing, hinting, weight appearance) so thinner or rougher text on Windows is expected rather than a bug
Explains that Helvetica Neue is not installed on Windows or most Android devices, so the fallback in the stack was used there, and that the designer's view is not what everyone sees
Recommends a stack with sensible per-platform fallbacks or a system font stack, or an explicitly shipped font, as the fix, with a CSS example
Gives a concrete pre-launch test list: real devices or services, a Windows machine, an old Android, normal and zoomed text, light and dark where relevant
Is honest that exact appearance can't be made identical everywhere and sets realistic expectations
